Yes, but if the Chamber would assist, let me say it in very general terms, in giving a proper understanding to the witness of his position and especially in view of the very small portion of the evidence that was given in private session, that there seems to be no objections. I'm also looking at other Defence counsel. No objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll deal with the matter outside Court and it might well be that I even have a Scandinavian person for you to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can talk with a Norwegian legal advisor for two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to the Croatian political structures in August 1995, did you have a good understanding of how the country was governed, its ministries, the powers of those ministries, how the country ran its legal institutions?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who should do that assessment, if I have a good understanding. I'm sure that my general understanding was that a -- at an okay level to perform my monitoring function, but I'm also sure that some even local people would say that I probably didn't even understand anything or some were to argue -- a good understanding is a little weak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I just put -- some people come along, Mr. Liborius, and think they know all about a country when they have been in effect - I don't say this disparagingly - a military tourist, and others come along and say, I didn't have an in-depth knowledge, I didn't know how the institutions worked but I was there faced with a job and a task. Do you understand what I'm getting at? And whether you can answer that question in those terms may assist us.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let's, for practical purposes, say that I had a reasonably fair understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. In relation to General Cermak, and we'll be returning to the questions I've just add you in a moment. In relation to General Cermak, you said you had meetings from time to time. I'm going to ask you to be more precise, as to how many meetings you had with him. We have seen, in evidence, two. Are you able to indicate more?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have more than two meetings with the General. It would, however, require a more in-depth scrutiny of reports to precisely say when. I have previously said that I -- and this is just off the top of my head, if you will accept that, a couple of times and discussed various issues. But I would really have to do a closer scrutiny, if -- to answer precisely to your question, when.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to set you a task, if I may, as we know your evidence won't be finished today and you will be returning to this Court, and I would like you, on your return, to provide me with a list of those dates of meetings you had with General Cermak, and any supporting evidence you may have to that effect. If you can't bring the supporting evidence, the list of the dates will do itself. And perhaps you could bring that when you return on the next occasion. Turning now to other matters, within the documents that you did bring here, am I right in saying the evidence only shows two meetings?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To your last question, I don't think that is a proper reflection of my material. Secondly, the task of producing an exact list of dates, let me remind what I have said before. I do not have control over the entire ECMM library. I therefore cannot perform such a task to the degree I believe would satisfy your request. However, if you -- I may offer a humble advice, I think that those who have control of the entire ECMM archive could discuss with you how that could best be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I think Mr. Kay invites you to see what you can do to the best of your abilities, no more, no less. Parties may do all kind of other investigative activities. There may be a lot of material already in the hands of the parties, perhaps even in evidence, but Mr. Kay is asking you to see what you can do in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And why I ask it is because it is not accepted from our side, Mr. Liborius, that you had regular or frequent meetings with General Cermak. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Turning, then, to your understanding of General Cermak, and you said you had a reasonable knowledge of Croatia, its military, its laws, are you able to tell me whether the position of military governor exists within the Croatian governmental system, military system, or anywhere for that matter as a concept within Croatia in 1995?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within my reasonable knowledge to perform my monitoring functions, I was not surprised to learn from different sources that a military governor had been put in place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: My question was, and I'll repeat it for you, is, whether, within the Croatian governmental system, military hierarchy, whether there is the position of military governor.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The full understanding of the entire complexity of the military and civilian structure would require a significant large knowledge I did not have. The military governor, his tasks, subordination and the like, such detailed knowledge was not available to me at the start of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So if the position of military governor did not exist and had no subordination or command, your theories and impressions at the time would be mistaken. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes. I think the witness can answer about what his factual observations were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can make objections against the question. This is a question that can be put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I believe it is argumentative.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it is. The witness may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not command the English language to a degree where I can fully understand your question. I would kindly ask you to be -- speaking with an English language that a non-native speaker -- Your theories of impression, could you be more specific, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think you understand my question entirely, sir, but I will deal with it in another way. You --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, no reason -- it's Friday, I'm aware of that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your theories and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, Mr. Liborius. Mr. Kay will rephrase the question in such a way. And if he finally does not succeed, then we, as non-native speakers, will see whether we can find a solution for it. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The reason why I asked the question, is you've made a statement, it's in evidence in this Court, and in fact you've made several statements and we're analysing what you said, whether you knew what you were talking about, and one of those statements is this: "His appointment alone indicates that he was in a specified area to direct and control what was the result after the operations had been finalised." Also in another statement: "I was asked about General Cermak's title." This statement was taken with Mr. Waespi being present. "It was my understanding at the time that Cermak's official title was military governor. This understanding was based on public information by Croatian authorities as well as on the title presented in meetings between the General and the ECMM." So your statement about the rank and position of General Cermak, you link with his authority to direct and control. Now, I am asking you where, in law, if you know that, within the Croatian system, this position is to be found; or did you not know what you were talking about?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the reference to the specific law. I think I know what I was talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So I'll go back to the original question. So if the position did not exist as you have described it, then you are mistaken or wrong about the powers that you said it would have. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are pretty high-flying here and I may ask for the non-native speaker's intervention, so if the -- so if the position did not exist as you described it ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's just play it simple.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think it is that complicated, Mr. Liborius. What Mr. Kay would like to know is that if your had no proper understanding of this position, whether that would have had, as a consequence, that your assessment of powers related to that position would be wrong. That's the simple question, if I understood Mr. Kay well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Hmm ... General Cermak described to me his role as being responsible for law and order, and I believe that I heard public broadcasts -- or other public information, suggesting that the title was military governor, and I think that I have seen correspondence, UN correspondence, and others, where the title was used. When Mr. Augarde had meetings with -- meeting with the General, I was not participating so I don't know what the General presented himself with, but I recall that in one of our reportings just around Operation Storm that the title was introduced. So I do think that the military governor understanding existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: To go back to the question, if you are wrong about this title of military governor and its control and authority, you have made an error in your description of his powers. Isn't that right? And I'll remind you that someone is on trial here.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I'm wrong, of course, then, what you suggest would be right. However, I do not think I'm wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you got any document or note anywhere where Mr. Cermak said that he was responsible for law and order in the region? We have looked at your diary, your notes, your meeting reports. Do you have a single record of a statement by him to you of that? If so, please produce it. Are you going to your statements to the Prosecution? Please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm going to my reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The problem is that I don`t have all my ECMM reports available. So --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall I set you another task, because I don't want us to be here all afternoon while you read all your reports. Could you produce a statement by him to you of that effect, if there is one. Thank you. Let's now look at what was printed and published about General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the first document I'd like the witness to see is D31.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 5th of August. It does concern the appointment of General Cermak by the President of Croatia and Supreme Commander of the armed forces, under the laws of the Republic of Croatia, and you'll see there that on the 5th of August, Reserve Colonel General Cermak was appointed to be the commander of the Knin garrison. And a Mr. Gojevic was appointed to be Deputy Commander of the Knin garrison. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is Mr. Cermak's appointment and the appointment that sent him to Knin. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But will you agree it doesn't say he was appointed as a military governor?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mentioned in that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we go to D36. Just in case you're harbouring thoughts that there may be some kind of secret appointment, we'll look at what the newspapers reported on the 6th of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm wondering whether we have to deal with it in this way. I think -- is there any dispute about what the formal position of Mr. Cermak was, Mr. Waespi, in this respect, such as military governor or ... whether he was the garrison commander? If not, then it can be put to the witness in rather short and clear terms, I would say, Mr. Kay, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I am hoping to do this quickly. I have a reason in actually going on this issue this way for the document after this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, but let's try to find most efficient ways of going through the material.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, this is a contest as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There we see the newspaper report: "President Tudjman appoints Ivan Cermak, headline commander of Knin." You will see in the fourth line, he is appointed commander of the Knin garrison, and you will see there, reference to him having been an advisor between 1990 and 1991 to the office of the President, assistant minister of defence, and, in 1993, minister of economy. Did you see any documents at the time from the Croatian side that established Mr. Cermak's appointment?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Croatian side, is that Croatian authorities or media report or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Croatian media, Croatian authorities. Were you interested in what they said Mr. Cermak was?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see any authorities' appointment. I believe that my understanding was, as I said before, based on broadcasts and I believe that I saw UN correspondence, you said Croatian correspondence, but I saw UN correspondence where it was mentioned, and I did not hear him protesting on that mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, do you understand this: If someone is wrong about something and passes it to someone else who is also given wrong information, that an incorrect impression can rapidly be passed from mouth to mouth. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And what I`m asking you is whether you think you have committed that same error, in relation to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Shall we look at the next document? 2D05-0088. This is a document written by you on the 24th of August, 1995, signed by you. And it concerns the harassment of a man called Dusan Drpa and you sending this letter to General Cermak. Do you see who you've sent it to there, the commander ZM, Knin, General Colonel Ivan Cermak. So not military governor, but the commander, ZM Knin. Can you explain that at all?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Cermak was referred to, to the best of my knowledge, as military governor. His formal title when addressing there, I think that I talked with -- was it some of the CALOs on his former title. It did not really, to my mind, at that time, made the big difference. I clearly see the address in the letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that the garrison HQ where General Cermak was working had under ten people working for him in there, under his control and authority? Did you know that? For these purposes?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- I won't delay court time, but D30 is a document that the Court knows which shows the staffing of the garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the previous document I failed to ask to be admitted as an exhibit. May I admit it, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D757.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D757 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Croatian army legal officers -- not legal officers. Croatian army liaison officers never referred to General Cermak as the military governor, did they?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: My recollection is that when the word "military governor" was used, that it was not immediately being rejected. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is the answer then --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- army liaison officers referring to him was usually just General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is the answer to the question: They never referred to him as military governor.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, may I ask you one question. It seems that the translation of the document that is the 24th August letter contains some handwritten comment at the bottom which I don't find in the original. Is that correct and could you perhaps then upload an uncommented translation?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's as it came.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We don't know who added anything but it seems not to be in the English original. Apparently in reference to EU or something like that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It had -- that part hasn't been translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it's the other way around. The English is -- at least in e-court, the English is the original, so something has been added to the translation which is not found in the original.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think Your Honour will find that the correspondence went in two languages. Remember with General Forand there was the English language document followed by a translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case then, of course I am misled by that apparently in the system we are talking about the original and translation where it appears to be two originals in two languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm going to look at a series of documents that look at General Cermak and his ability to try and subordinate individuals or even a collection of soldiers, a unit under him. The first document I'm going to look at is 65 ter 5033. This was a document that the Prosecution had put in a proposed bar table Cermak docs file but not the following documents that I will also be referring to. The first document is dated the 9th of August, 1995. And you can see that it's an order from General Cermak considering the situation within the Knin ZM. Did you know what ZM stands for within the Croatian military?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Garrison command. And it's a particular function within the Croatian military system.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the logistics support to Croatian army units and civilian organs of the Knin ZM, and you can see the order, that a -- the commander of the 306th is to temporarily assign a man called Zeljko Jonjic as a temporary replacement, and that order is even delivered to General Gotovina, the 306th commander and a sector commander of the 306th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And it is, as I said, Your Honour, a document that the Prosecution rely upon. Let us now go to 2D05-0086.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And coming up will be a document dated the 12th of August, from the 306th logistic base in Split, where Mr. Jonjic, the subject of the previous order, was based. And it's from the commander of that unit, and he sends this order to the Split Military District commander, General Gotovina. And he doesn't send it to the Knin ZM. And it says, about the commander of the 306th logistic base, Major Jonjic leaving his duty of his own will and making himself available to the Knin garrison commander and at the order of the Knin garrison commander by which the system of the command in the 306th has been seriously disrupted. And then he orders that a Lieutenant Mirkov shall take Jonjic's post and that post shall remain until the emerged situation is solved and possible disciplinary procedure is terminated. And then some orders that go with it. Before I ask you any further questions, were you aware of the structure of the Split Military District, of the units within it, the hierarchy, the identities of the officers, commanders?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to this document, you agree that that is a complaint by the Commander Pavic about the order putting Major Jonjic within the Knin garrison. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the document before. I can read it up but I can't really ascertain the status of the document. It's the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just take it that's an original, all these documents are original. They come from the military files. Let's look at the next document, dated 2D05 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May the previous document be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D758.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D758 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if we could pull up 2D05-0082.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, before we do so the break will be at 2.00. If you can manage in two minutes, fine; if not --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's what I'm aiming to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 16th of August and we see now not an order by General Cermak to some major in the 306th logistic base but a notice to him and saying: "Dear Mr. Commander, Ivan Pavic." He refers to the order of Major Pavic on the 12th of August and to unnecessary insinuations concerning Major Zeljko Jonjic's leaving of the duty on his own will. And as he says: "As you already know, on my order and as agreed with the Split Military District commander Colonel General Gotovina, Major Jonjic is temporarily assigned to Knin garrison, where he carries out the tasks extremely well. If needed by Colonel General Gotovina, he will return to his position of the Sibenik logistics base commander." Do you understand the thrust of this picture of the orders, Mr. Liborius, concerning the authority and control that General Cermak really had in Knin? Do you understand why we're looking at it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I understand why we're looking at it. The General, in dealings with not only the UN or ECMM or other visitors, was given as the point of contact when it came to law and order. There was a distinction between General Gotovina and General Cermak. And we certainly used him as the point of contact. I have not seen these papers before. I think I understand -- I think I understand why you are showing the papers, but what I can say is that in our monitoring capacity locally, he even invited me to phone him if we encountered any problems, if we encountered irregularities. He even gave me his phone number so that when there was a problem I should call him and I saw, with the soldiers in the field during the month of August, that his authority was known to the soldiers. Whether he had ten in his command, I will not comment on that. What in effect saw was a person with a title -- a rank of a General who was known to those locally. The agents of the Croatian authorities, mainly military. So for me, he exercised control. His words were important. If we could proceed our patrols or we had to be stopped, I called the General or his staff frequently. I even put his phone number in the first page of my patrol notebook so that I could, with very little problem, find the phone number and dial it, and I saw that it worked. You asked me about, if I know -- if I knew at that time his command, I will rely on what the General told us. I'm not so particularly -- at that time interested in the inner fine mechanics of the Croatian system. He was, as I said, the point of contact. It even developed to the level where, when they were visiting ambassadors accredited to Zagreb, that he was the person they should speak to. So I gathered that he exercised a great deal of authority. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, and Mr. Kay as well, two minutes become seven. We will have a break and resume at a quarter to 3.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 2.06 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I was glad to hear that the conversation with Mr. Nilsson has had a good result. Mr. Kay, are you ready to continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Two housekeeping matters. Might the document 65 ter 5033 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D759.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D759 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And the last document I raised, 2D05-0082, may that be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D760.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D760 is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we look at a document 65 ter 534. This is a document dated the 11th of August, 1995. Again, it's from General Cermak. It's from the Knin garrison. And it's in accordance with the operational needs in the Knin garrison command. And under the laws of the Republic of Croatia, this, again, for Mr. Waespi's benefit, is one of those bar table docs. We can see an order being issued here to the commander of the 142nd Home Guard Regiment. And it is a temporary assignment to the Knin garrison command from the ranks of the 33 and we see names there of individuals, Cacic, Rajcic, Konfota, Kaligar, Kovic, Mjakovic, Krvavica. Let's go now to 65 ter 4599, which was not part of the bar docs. This is dated the 21st of August, 1995. It's, again, a document from General Cermak, for the attention of General Gotovina. It is a request because of the operative requirements of Knin garrison, and in order to expedite the process of getting the city back to normal. Just stopping there, did you in fact understand that that was the specific task of General Cermak, was the process of getting the city back to normal. Did you know that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I see this document. Getting the city back to normal, it fits quite well with the General's words to international organisations being responsible for law and order. So I think that -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did he say he was responsible for law and order?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my belief, he said that in meetings with senior UN officials shortly after having taken up office, and I believe that he, in the meeting with Mr. Augarde, and I think it's produced in one of the ECMM documents, said among other things that he would propose a guard to be posted at our office, among other things. So establishing law and order, I believe, was a part of his brief, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: First of all, were you present in any UN meeting where that was said?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Secondly, are you seriously suggesting that arranging the guard on the office of the ECMM makes you responsible for the law and order of an entire region? Is that your considered judgement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, among other things, that indicates that a range of issues was discussed in Mr. Augarde's meeting, and I actually do consider that taking the -- taking the operational decision, having the compatibility to taking the operational decision to say, I will put a guard in front of a large international organisation's main office in Knin, such a decision, you would not take, unless you had the responsibility for the law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll look further, then, at these documents. This is the request for 65 conscripts to be placed under the command of the Knin garrison commander. Do you understand the terms of what that is? That is saying, I don't have the power to direct those conscripts to come and work for me so I'm asking you to give them to me. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I see the letter, 21st of August, I understand that. The reference I made was to the meeting he had with Colonel Augarde. And I think it would clarify my answer if we could bring that up document. Maybe the Prosecutor could help us. It's the report of Mr. Augarde speaking about guards.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Prosecutor will re-examine you and I will ask you which documents to look at, and I will ask you the questions. Do you understand that? And time is important in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may 65 ter 534 be made an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D761.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D761 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May 65 ter 4599 also be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D762.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D762 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document we will look at is 65 ter 2989.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 22nd of August, the day following. And it's to the commander of the 142nd Home Guard Regiment. And it's from General Gotovina to that commander, and it's pursuant to the request of the commander of the Knin garrison, General Cermak, for the purpose of faster and more effective organisation of a normal life in the town. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you would look at these documents rather than other documents whilst I'm questioning you. The order is that the commander of the 142nd temporarily, until further notice, singles out from the 33 of the 142nd Home Guard, and resubordinate to the commander, typed here Knin command post, meaning garrison command, the list of soldiers being enclosed. And they're to report on a certain day, on the 25th, and receive specific tasks. And there we see various related orders. And on page 2 of the English, you can see signed by General Gotovina, who it is to be sent to, including the garrison command, and there's a list of 69 soldiers from Knin and from Kijevo, a list of 78 soldiers. If on the Croatian version we turn to page 2, we will see a list of names. And I'd like to point out the name at number 1, Mojmir Rojcic; the name at 11, Josef Cacic; the name at 16, Bozo Kaligera; and the name at 44, Davor Kovic, which links back to the exhibit I produced earlier dated the 11th August, which was 65 ter 534, marked as D761. We've no need to call it up because we will waste time, but I do that for the Court's benefit. The point I'm making to you here, Mr. Liborius, is that a commander who is unable to subordinate troops to himself is not the commander with the authority and control that you have described. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see these documents for the first time. In August -- what is the date, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Last one is the 22nd of August.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And the request for further personnel would indicate, for me, at this point in time, 2008, that either the tasks are being expanded or, as you would suggest, insufficient personnel are available to the present tasks. Which of the two, I simply cannot decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You don't see this, because your words "insufficient personnel are available to the present tasks," you don't see this, then, that if he is the commander with authority and control over the troops in the region, this Colonel General could have just issued an order himself to get these conscripts to clean up the streets of Knin. Don't you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You are inviting me to give my answer here and, as I also said to Mr. Misetic, I'm not second-guessing. In my profession, unless I have an uninterrupted, at my own decision, selected set of documents indicating --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, Mr. Liborius, the question was whether you did agree with Mr. Kay. I do hear that you do not agree. Just tell him, I do not agree. And then, if Mr. Kay wants further explanation, he will ask you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say that I agreed or not agreed. I said I was not a position to make a decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So then you do not agree. That is, either because you cannot make up your mind that is a reason not to agree or because you think you are sufficiently informed to disagree, but you certainly did not agree. That is clear from your answer. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. Let's look at another document, 65 ter, which was on the proposed Cermak bar table docs, 1736.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And perhaps we assign numbers if they've not yet received a number and that would then be P numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would be grateful if they would be D numbers, Your Honour, in fact, because I'm producing them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh you --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just -- it was a mistake on my part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm not being possessive. It's just easier for us to organise our affairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 1736. From the Knin garrison, 12th August, 1995, urgent clearing of the military depot in Plavno with the aim of making the return of the population to this settlement as flexible and fast as possible. I hereby issue the following order. Ordered by General Cermak, the terrain should be cleared, or the facility should be cleared, and he names a man, Lieutenant Andjelko Vuk - apologies for any mispronunciation. It gives what he is responsible for. There's a commission, a Colonel Frkic; Major Gojevic, whom we've seen D -- Exhibit D31 was the Deputy Commander of the garrison; and Colonel Emir Teskeredzic. And we can see that this document was sent to those individuals, the assistant commander for logistics of the Knin garrison, and a section of the 306th LOB, Sibenik. That order happens on the 12th August. Let's look --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D763.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D763 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document is 65 ter 2973, dated the 22nd of August, 1995. While that is coming up, Your Honour, may 65 ter 2989 be exhibited. I don't think I've done that. That was the list of the names of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D764.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D764 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I apologise for not doing this in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document, dated the 22nd of August, is from Colonel Cermak to the 1st Croatian Guard Corps, to the commander, Colonel General Cuk and a request for temporary transfer because of the exceptional need to carry out explosive ordnance, clearing of the terrain and facilities. And we see the name, Major Andjelko Vuk, given a different rank than the previous order. But we see that name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I ask the Court to note that. May that be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D765.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D765 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Moving now to 65 ter 3411. This is a document dated the 20th of September, 1995, containing the first name on the Croatian document that should be looked at, Brigadier Emin Teskeredzic. Different spelling but, in fact, evidence will be same person in the previous orders. This is a document from the Knin -- from the commander of the Split Military District, General Gotovina, concerning pyrotechnical restoring of ground and buildings and removal of mines. Page 2 of the English where you're at already. We see the people mobilised, we see that they're to report to the Knin garrison command, to be received by General Cermak and a report to be sent to the Split Military District command, to a particular section. Page 3 of the English concludes that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Again, Mr. Liborius, this General that you said had authority and control is unable to subordinate or command particular troops under his authority. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't seen the documents before. It would indicate that there is a need to have further personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But your statements, Mr. Liborius --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Liborius, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- said that you believed, it was your opinion that General Cermak, remaining behind in Knin, was in control of the troops. That's what you said in your statement to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Und?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you, in fact, realize that that statement was wrong, do you accept it, that that was wrong?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What my statement was based on was my observations, information from meetings, from trustworthy colleagues and those were the facts I saw them on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, Mr. Kay is asking is whether -- now having seen these documents whether you would reconsider that assessment you made at the time on the basis, as you said. That is simply the question. Could be yes, could be no. Please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's look at the next document, 65 ter 1791. And it concerns the guarding of facilities, something that you mentioned only 15 minutes ago. And we'll look at how General Cermak was able to deal with it, shall we? It's a document dated the 19 August 1995. It's to the Chief of Staff of the Split Military District. It's from General Cermak, and its subject is securing manpower for safeguard purposes, request. "Since, from the time when Knin was liberated, it is necessary to engage, on a daily basis, a number of people to safeguard the military and civilian facilities in Knin, and as with the consent of the commander of the Split Military District, 25 military conscripts from the 6th Home Guard Regiment ... have temporarily been redeployed and have ... performed security tasks since the 11th of August." And there's a proposal, to secure relief in the following manner and to reassign military conscripts who lived in Knin, in the area before the war to members of that particular company and their action would have the effect on the performance of other necessary tasks within the Knin command post. And then it says: "If the above-stated cannot be implemented, please secure the relief for the manpower of the 6th Home Guard Regiment with ... 25 military conscripts from another unit or with new manpower, from the 6th Home Guard Regiment ..." Page 2, that is signed by General Cermak. You see, he doesn't even have the power to organise himself and take out troops to guard facilities, military and civilian, and, I dare say, your office may have been one of them, without requesting someone else in the military structure to do it. Do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do see requests for additional personnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But it's the point of the request, Mr. Liborius, and that answer is disingenuous, isn't it? You know it's the point of the request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe that the witness testified several times that he bases what he says in conclusions on the observations he made at that time on the ground. And I've -- I see where counsel is going. We can gone on for 10, 15, 20 more documents. I'm not -- whether it makes sense to ask the witness for each document again for his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, the conclusions you've given, as you said, Mr. Liborius, on the basis of what you observed at the time are of a rather broad nature, isn't it. Now what Mr. Kay is doing, he is putting to you that there is documentary evidence which Mr. Kay considers to be in contradiction with your assessment at that time. He is putting it to you, because, I think he considers it fair, that before perhaps at a later stage he'll criticise and he will challenge your testimony as we find it in your statement, that he finds it fair that he puts to you at this moment the documents which are, in his assessment, in contradiction with or inconsistent with your testimony. That's what he is doing. I couldn't say that perhaps it could be done a bit more quickly, but apart from that, Mr. Waespi, that is fundamental fairness also to the witness, not only to the accused but also to the witness, because apparently Mr. Kay disagrees with the conclusions and assessments Mr. Liborius made. So if you would, please, carefully look at the documents, if you see something which you say, Well, this -- of course, you're not in a position to check whether -- what is right in the documents, but if you'd just briefly answer Mr. Kay as, Well, on the basis of this I will not change my conclusions or to say, Well, I'm not in a position to give -- to have -- I'm not in a position to be able to compare all the documents with what I've seen, so I refrain from an expression on whether I agree or whether I disagree. Then we can move forward rather quickly. I hope so. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would prefer that formulation you just gave, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. If that is what you want to say and of course the formulation is -- is well chosen, I do agree with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think it is excellent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, it is important that you tell Mr. Kay what your position is. Not the nicest formulation but what is closest to what you consider your answer would be to his question. Mr. Kay, perhaps we proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, I am concerned about Mr. Waespi's intervention and I'll just make a brief statement about it. This is important for us and our case. We have seen documents being taken out of context and we are just examining what is behind it. And as Your Honours know, this witness's evidence is challenged in a very strong way as to his conclusions. We're not criticizing him but it's how he came to his point of view and the other evidence in the case that we feel this Tribunal should be able to receive, see, and hear and compare what the witness says about it. Your Honour is quite right --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Your statement is on the record. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there it is. That's 65 ter 1791. May that be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D766, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D766 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I also have admitted 65 ter 3411, which I neglected to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As D767, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D767 is also admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: 65 ter 2416, please. A document dated the 19th of October, 1995. It's signed by the chief of the Croatian army Main Staff, General Cervenko. Did you know General Cervenko at all?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. The document is to the sector for training and schooling. And its subject is carrying out work at the Knin garrison headquarters. And it's an order. And that order, on that date, is for the organisation of 200 soldiers in the military training centre to be sent to Knin garrison HQ, to assist in cleaning the town and to provide the vehicles for them. So, again, showing, Mr. Liborius, that this commander that you said had authority and control in the region, again, couldn't order troops to be subordinated under him. Don't you agree?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hmm ... I am not in a position to check whether my position to these documents so I will refrain from expressing whether I agree or not. I kindly reproduce the words of Your Honour, Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Are you the sort of man, Mr. Liborius, that even when he has evidence staring him in the face refuses to acknowledge it? Are you someone who has difficulty in accepting when you are wrong?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, is this question relate -- this -- I'm not really sure how I should relate to that question at all. Is that a psychological profile, because then I'm perfectly happy to take a psychological test.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's not -- Mr. Kay, as a matter of fact, although he does that in the language lawyers do use in court, actually asks you whether you find it difficult, if the documentary evidence would contradict what you said, whether, in general, you have difficulties in admitting that. If that would be the case, please say yes; if that is not the case, please say no. At the same time, please would you first answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to answer that question, let just play with some ideas that it has been possible for me to hide my innermost personal characters as a senior Danish civil servant for more than 20 years. That would be very, very special. So I do not consider myself the sort of man that, even when he has evidence staring him in his face refusing to acknowledge it. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, would you refrain from making this courtroom a bit of a debating room. And Mr. Kay, I know the art of advocacy. There are also limits to that. Some questions might not really assist the Chamber --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have understood, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in making determinations, so -- Mr. Liborius, Mr. Kay is going to put his next question to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can I make that document an exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D768.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Yes, Mr. Liborius, you want to say something. At the same time, you will have an opportunity at the end of your testimony to add anything that has been -- you said so. Okay. Then 15 seconds.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first question I was put by Mr. Misetic when I came here was: Why did I start taking notes in this room? How is that question to be interpreted, as an insult?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, it is not to be interpreted as an insult. And if there is any question which would be inadmissible, Mr. Waespi, as he has shown several times, will object against the question. And if you have listened well, then I said something about the questions one minute ago to Mr. Kay. So, please, rely on Mr. Waespi, a bit on me as well, and the professionality of Defence counsel. Let's not further discuss the matter. Mr. Kay, your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have 65 ter 535, please. This is a document dated the 11th of August, by General Cermak to the Ministry of Defence, transport and technical administration. It's a request for vehicles for the purpose of organizing work in the area of the Knin garrison command. We request the following vehicles be provided urgently. And then there's a request for vehicle for food transport, pick-up truck, refrigerator truck. We can see the sorts of material being sought and asking for them to be delated to the Knin garrison command. So an example there of where the commander can't even requisition his own vehicles from anywhere. Do you see that? Do you agree with that.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that. I, with regard to whether I agree, will say I'm not in a position to check -- in this -- the formulation of Your Honour, the Judge. I will use the same phrase as before, Your Honour. So I will refrain from expressing whether I agree or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you don't have an opinion on it, is that right? Looking at this document here and the sequence of the other documents doesn't cause you to doubt anything that you have said before in your statements?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will repeat the sentence from before, so I will refrain from expressing whether I agree or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was not the question. The question was now, whether what you see at this moment, whether that creates any doubt in your mind as far as the conclusions are concerned you have drawn in your examination-in-chief and in your statements. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not changed my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you shown any documentary evidence such as this? Was the background to the case explained to you at all?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we make that document an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D769.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D769 is admitted. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have a whole series of documents here relating to some UN vehicles that were taken, stolen, from the UN, and Croatian army soldiers were seen driving them. I'm not going to go into them. But were you aware of that issue, that there had been a theft of many UN vehicles that General Forand complained about and complained to General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was an issue of vehicles. I think I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that, in fact, General Cermak couldn't deal with that matter. He had to write to a higher authority and get help for those vehicles to be looked for. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If you had been aware of it, wouldn't it indicate to you that he didn't have the authority and control that you've claimed he had from your knowledge at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The indication as to control of the vehicles, I can come up with a lot of speculations, who could be having a wish to maintain these vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Here we are. So within the structure of the Croatian military, do you know where the garrison command would be positioned, where it would be placed?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Outside the operational command.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And would you be aware of to whom it was subordinated, the garrison command?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would ask if I had any doubts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you ask anyone about the garrison command, as to where it fitted within the Croatian military structure at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information from General Cermak did not lead me or my colleagues, as I believe, to ask such a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So is the answer to that no?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not answer -- ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, there we are. Within the civil authorities of the Croatian republic, did you have any idea of the hierarchy controlling the civil police?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you talking names or are you talking structures?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Structures.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chiefs of police, in their information to me, said that they were subordinated to higher authorities in the civilian administrative, corresponding to the civilian administrative structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would that be the Ministry of Interior?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police was, to my knowledge, subordinated to the Ministry of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we just produce P500 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document already in evidence showing the organisation of the Ministry of Interior, and the structure of the civil police.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we enlarge it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, the minister of interior, Mr. Jarnjak. Were you aware of him being in that position?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Going further down this hierarchy, can you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we scroll down a bit please. Thank you very much. Just there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you see Ivica Cetina who was chief of the Zadar-Knin police administration?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, can I see his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was aware of the Zadar-Knin police administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question was were you aware of him.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The name rings a bell, but I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Moving further down, Knin-Kotar police administration, Mr. Cedo Romanic. Did he ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in the Knin police station waiting for a meeting with the chief of police, and as we were waiting, I believe that he came, had a short but unproductive talk, so Mr. Zvonko Gambiroza was the main part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, you give an answer -- the question simply was did you ever meet him and you give all kind of detail --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Technically, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you just give the short answers. I mean you are concerned about time. So are we. So whether Mr. Kay is interested to know the date or who else was there or whether the meeting was productive -- if you just give a short answer, then Mr. Kay will put his question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The bottom line we see the names of commanders of various police stations. First of all, did you visit any or all of those police stations. Just say any or all; don't give me the detail.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any or all, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, that -- was that all of them, did you visit?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gracac, Donji Lapac, Knin, Obrovac, Lovinac, Korenica, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So some you visited --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Some you visited; others you didn't. Did you know the commander of Knin police station, Mr. Mijic?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had heard his name. I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you appreciate that there was a police station commander in each of those places and that that was subordinated to the Knin-Kotar police administration?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And that that, in turn, was subordinated to the Zadar-Knin police administration as well?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And so it went up the chain to the minister of interior himself. Did you understand that there was a strict hierarchical system?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you know that that police system, as the civil authority, was put into action straight away from the 4th of August, by the minister of interior and his assistant ministers? Did you appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw the police in their locations right after.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you appreciate that the police station at Knin, the Knin-Kotar police station was opened on the 6th of August by the minister of interior, Mr. Jarnjak?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who opened it. I know that it was opened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And did you appreciate that the Zadar-Knin police administration was immediately running the affairs of the civil police in a supervisory aspect to the Knin-Kotar police administration?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That corresponds to my observation in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've seen many documents in this Court that evidence that, Mr. Liborius, but I'm asking you these questions because in your statement, you said that Mr. Cermak was in control until the elections, and that he was in control of the law and order until the elections had taken place. Do you remember saying that in your statement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Now, have you got any note of him saying that, from any meeting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information from General Cermak to the ECMM was dealt with in some of the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I asked if you had a note. You can just say yes or no. And if you don't --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to look.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because I haven't seen that --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have it right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I haven't seen a note and I would have expected if there had been a note that that would have been brought to certainly the Court's attention and my attention, from any document that you had. But it's not there, is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness has answered that question, Mr. Kay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I'm dealing with it is for this reason: That it is simply not a fact based on any truth. Do you understand me? Because it -- there was no question of elections affecting the authority of the civil police. The Croatian government had a system in place, up and running, right from the start. They had their own control of the police within the Ministry of Interior. Cermak was nothing to do with that. So would you like to revise your recollection of this matter? Would you like to think about it again, whether it was ever said in that way at all?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to revise my recollection of my monitoring observations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But do you see how it doesn't make any sense for him to have said that? Do you see that, how it would be totally illogical?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: How I see sense -- I would like to give you two examples so that you see how I see sense, if you ask me about sense.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, I'm asking about the logic of this statement, whether you can see it as not actually fitting any of the political structures, governmental structures. You told us had you a reasonable knowledge. I asked you that at the start. You said you had had training in it, that you understood it reasonably.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, when General Cermak met with EU's most senior people, he was given the expression of being the point of contact for law and order. Let me just explain to you - and you have taken considerable time up of my patience to explain how the system was. Let me explain how the system looked like and I want to bring two examples, only two examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: One very low.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- I would just appreciate it if you'd --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and one very high.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- just answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Briefly. Very briefly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: One very low example, experienced by myself, out in the field where a -- on the 1st of September, 1995, I am detained by --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What date?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1st of September, 1995, I am detained at a little after 1415. I make a phone call to the operations centre, the ECMM operations centre, saying I am kept. There is a call made, I believe from the operations centre to General Cermak, and very short after, I can proceed. That was the low example. The high example.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Stop there.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was given two examples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I gave Mr. Liborius, briefly, the second one.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a Troika visit - we are now on 19 October. The Troika visit is the expression when the three EU ambassadors from the presiding EU country, the next and the third visit. This is Carl Bildt's people in the field. Now Mr. Misetic argued with a letter from Mr. Mate Granic that it was important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no. You give --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was then discussing matters of security, matters of return, matters of property lists and so on. He is selected by the Croatian government to be the point of contact when the EU's entire power structure comes to town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that was your second example. Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And I don't disagree with point of contact, by the way.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But the question I was asking you, which seems a long way away, but let's just go back to your two examples and I will have a look at them with you. Let's go to the 1st of September. Do you know where Mr. Cermak was on the 1st of September?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He wasn't in Knin. He was in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, a phone call was made, I believe, from the OPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So you believe a phone call was made to someone and then someone speaks to someone and you get released?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- as I said before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, if we have any detailed further information about it we'd like to hear; if not, let's move on. Let's not start talking about how logical it is to phone someone, either on a cell phone or whether any satellite phone, or whether the phone call was long or short. Let's move on, unless there is real information more than what the witness has told us. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I was challenging the witness on his thought process but I will leave that for later argument, with the Court's leave, but the Court knows it is a matter which I challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Let's just look at the freedom of movement that you say is so important on -- on this matter. First of all, that doesn't indicate, that fact, that there is any control or authority over troops, does it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a radio relayed or a telephone instruction is relayed that really does indicate control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you know who was spoken to when the radio contact was made?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier on, we were issued a set of phone numbers, either to phone General Cermak or people in his staff. As I said, I phoned, and I believe that I reproduce information from yesterday, I phoned my operations office, and they took control of the matter, contacting either General Cermak or his staff. I received an information return, everything is okay, and I could proceed. That does indicate some sort of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In relation to freedom of movement, did you have any dealings with a Brigadier Plestina in Zagreb?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we see his name, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: P-l-e-s-t-i-n-a?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Plestina in Zagreb, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've heard evidence about this before. Brigadier Plestina was the general in the Croatian army who was the commander of the liaison officers with the UN and the ECMM. Did you know about him?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard his name in that connection, yes. I did not meet him myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have his phone number?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he make himself available to you as a contact in any way?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that as it was delegated down, and a general, Mr. Gotovina, gave his phone number, that would suffice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The answer, therefore, is simply no, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please just answer the question. No, no, no further debates, no further discussions. This is an invitation. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that the ECMM was not included within various orders concerning freedom of movement in the Knin region but they were documents that only affected UNCRO. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a specific freedom of movement document referring to you as the ECMM and giving you freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The freedom of movement cards as it was referred to, was it yesterday, I think by Mr. Misetic in the ECMM report, the go-anywhere card, that is the first example. The second example of an order that concerned ECMM was that Philippe Augarde in his meeting with General Cermak were granted -- were promised freedom of movement. So that was, I think, an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No. Did you have a piece of paper issued by General Cermak or anyone else dictating that you had freedom of movement or restricting your freedom of movement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remembered we had the card. It was the size of the -- it was called the go-anywhere card ensuring freedom of movement or at least providing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who issued that card?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have the card right at my disposal here. I am sure, however, that it could be obtained perhaps from the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm asking who issued it. Was it a document issued by the Croatian government from Zagreb, was it a local document from Knin?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a Zagreb government -- Zagreb document, to the best of my knowledge -- memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Right. So the card or document you were using to travel around the region was not issued by General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment. Is it 4.00, our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As a matter of fact, I -- yesterday, I think I -- I gave a list of times and I asked this afternoon to get it back. I think it was ten minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm grateful to Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So when you were stopped at a check-point, you would produce that authorisation to the particular troops on the point to say that you were entitled to pass. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sometimes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And if you say that if you had a problem, you would then phone General Cermak's office to try and get round your problem. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Typical instances where the card was produced but did not solve the situation, we would phone either General Cermak or his staff, using the phone numbers given to us by him, and that would usually solve the problem, resulting in instructions to the local authorities at the check-point to grant us freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, they`re hardly -- just granting you an absolute freedom of movement, what's happening here is that the unit who stopped you is checking on whether you are able to move around the country, aren't they, to move past that check-point. It's as simple as that.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember a couple of instances where it was not the unit who stopped us that did the checking. I did the checking with staff of Mr. Cermak's, and then, sometimes, handed the phone to the check-point personnel and that solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, I guess the impression that you did not understand the question well. The question by Mr. Kay was, I think - but please correct me Mr. Kay - is whether such a telephone call and being let through, whether that was an expression of a total freedom of movement or just a decision that you could pass that check-point. That was, I think, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was a decision at that individual point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And you never actually spoke to General Cermak yourself on the phone, did you?
