utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember I had notes where it says, Speaking to General Cermak solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that to the office or to General Cermak as an individual?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When he gave me his phone number, I think that the second or third instance of restriction of movement I got him, and it solved the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That phone number was not his mobile phone number, was it? It was the garrison command number.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number I have noted in my diary was 021375653.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we turn to P364, please, and turn to the second page of this document, produced in evidence through General Forand. It concerns the 12th of August, 1995. And if you could go to the bottom of the page you will see that there was a meeting between the commander of Sector South - that's General Forand - Brigadier Plestina, head of the office of UN and ECMM. We can see a discussion that took place outlined at A; we can see it also at B.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May we turn to page 3, and point C, where there is a discussion between General Forand about freedom of movement and Brigadier Plestina pledged full freedom of movement but indicated other issues were outside of his competence. Were you present at that meeting of the Brigadier at Sector South with General Forand?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware of that meeting?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that General Forand had a series of meetings to discuss freedom of movement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you aware that Brigadier Plestina was stating what the terms of freedom of movement would be to the UNCRO forces?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that Brigadier Plestina was dealing with the freedom of movement issues, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And he also - and we've seen evidence of this in documents produced by General Forand which we have no need to labour on here. I refer them --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honours, D318, Exhibit D319, and Exhibit D321.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: -- was telling the UN forces whether they had freedom of movement or not. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do we miss something on the screen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- well, whether there is anything on the screen missing, could you please answer the question put by Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could I have the question again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Of course. The Court is aware through other evidence of a series of meetings between Brigadier Plestina and the UN Chief of Staff in Zagreb as well as this meeting in Knin with General Forand in which Brigadier Plestina was telling the UN how their movements were restricted and what freedom of movement they would have. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of contacts between General Forand and Plestina. The specific meeting there, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's whether he was telling the UN commander what their restrictions of movement and freedom of movement would be.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Brigadier Plestina also, with the ECMM, similarly dictate what any restrictions of movement or freedoms of movement would be?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would imagine that the headquarter ECMM would be in contact. I don't have the specific information myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And at that level, none of that was to do with General Cermak, was it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As it was put to me locally, General Cermak would be the authority at our level to whom we should address those questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And who told you that? Was that General or Colonel Augarde?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Augarde, I believe, had that issue in his first meeting, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, I'm looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have got one short question to finish this subject, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please not again -- not a two-minute question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I will head anything off at the pass if I feel it is getting too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please put that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So it simply comes to this, you're stopped at a check-point, you need help, your pass comes from a ministry in Zagreb, and your point of contact who helps you out, you telephone the office of General Cermak, you may or may not speak to him, and then something is said and you're allowed on your way. Simple as that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll have a break. We will resume at 25 minutes to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May we have 65 ter 2971, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 22nd of August, 1995, from the military police administration -- military police department. And it's sent to the Split 72nd Military Police Battalion for action, the Knin garrison command, Colonel Cermak -- Colonel General Cermak for information. And it concerns the security of the Knin garrison commander, General Cermak, on the basis of analysis and with a view to continued protection for the Knin garrison command commander, General Cermak, while stationary and in motion. An order is made that the 72nd Military Police Battalion commander shall organise the task of protection of General Cermak, using men from the military police Knin 7th Company. A meeting would be held. And then on the next page, page 3 in the English, various other directions and it comes from Colonel Kozic. And so this is an order that even in terms of the military police, General Cermak had insufficient authority even to order someone for his personal protection or a number of men for his personal protection, and that had to be a task ordered by the separate part of the military police structure. Do you see that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And do you understand the significance of a document such as that, concerning the command and control of the military police?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command and control of military police, in general, would be significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you understand the significance, though, in terms of the actual authority of General Cermak, if he is unable to command a military police battalion to provide for his own security, that company, to carry out the task, even being in Knin, the 7th Company. Do you appreciate the significance of the restrictions on his authority?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall having associated General Cermak with command of military police. Nor was it brought to me in my monitoring duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, it's the significance of it, in terms of authority. It's the last time I will ask the question because you have written statements giving your views, opinions, how you believe things to be, and here I am putting a fact in front of you and asking for you -- if you're here to assist the Court to do so. If you're here to assist the Judges, all of us, please think about it and answer.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have thought about the issue of command of the military police, and I, never in my monitoring capabilities, and I believe that that is what my testimony is about, expect -- expected that the military police would be under General Cermak's command. I don't think that in the regular army structures it is so, so I don't see that as being a particular Croatian problem, as you would indicate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we can go do D281, and may the last document, while this is being called up, be admitted into evidence, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that becomes Exhibit number D770.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D770. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The next document, when it appears on the screen, is an order for an active defence, issued by the Split Military District commander, dated 9th of August, 1995. We're not going to look at all the pages of this document, because the Judges have seen it already. And what I want the usher -- sorry, the clerk of the Court to do is to turn to the last page of the document. And if we could blow that up. I think that that's a blurred copy there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: But that is an organigram of the organisational chart of the Split Military District and you knew the Split Military District was the particular forces that you were dealing with in the Knin region. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forces under Split was in our area, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. You were aware the Split Military District, were you, was the particular forces in the area that you were dealing with?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were dealing with a host of forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just tell me if you're aware of the Split Military District, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of the Split Military District, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Fine. In this organigram here, which sets out the composition of the forces and their structure, there isn't actually within it the Knin ZM, the Knin garrison command. All right? Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry to say I can't see the details. But if you say there is no Knin ZM, I'll take that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Take it from me. And if we can go to the previous page as to where this document is delivered to, we will see those who receive the particular plan, or strategy. I don't know whether you recognise any of those military brigades or battalions or any of the detail within it. Do you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just, in the interests of time, say 72nd MP battalion strikes my eyes immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've just looked at one of their orders.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you also notice the fact that the Knin ZM isn't included within that order?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, aware of the fact that this is a poorly reproduced organigram, the Defence have magnified one and it is at 2D05-0009. It's the same last page, but reproduced through technology in a clear form which we asked to be admitted as an exhibit linking it, as we do and for the record, with Exhibit 281. May it be admitted into evidence, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Waespi.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D771, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D771 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why I'm asking you these questions, Mr. Liborius, is because it is to do with the authority and command and control of troops. You said earlier that you were here just as -- about ECMM, but you're not. Your evidence is being adduced by the Prosecution through you on particular issues. Do you understand? My questioning doesn't confine myself just to the ECMM but to matters that are relevant to this trial, do you understand? That is why I'm asking you these questions.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I certainly also relate to issues outside the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Could we look at 65 ter 547, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 11th of August, 1995, issued by General Gotovina. It concerns the Split Military District command Sajkovici forward command post. And is an order on the basis of an arisen need to regroup the troops on the front line, establishing zones of responsibility and to ensure efficient command. And we see there an order about the 12th of August that the commands of the following temporary formations ceasing to function, their place is identified, and then commands shall be established and begin functioning, identifying the particular regiments, brigades? And then in 3, on the 12th of August, 1995, the Split Military District commands Zadar forward command post shall become the primary place from where to command all units of the Split Military District. We see on page of the English, in paragraph 4, a forward command post of the Split Military District command shall be set up in Knin. And it -- the order is made to begin preparations for that transfer and a date is given. The Chief of Staff of the Split Military District command and commanders of the directly subordinated units responsible for the implementation of this order. You will see there a list of the particular brigades, battalions, the Operational Groups identified in the order. You will also see garrisons, and you will see the garrisons of Zadar, Sinj, and Split. Not included is the Knin garrison, ZM. Do you understand what I mean by that, do you now, about the Knin ZM? The Knin Zborno Mjesto being the garrison command. Do you understand that, Mr. Liborius?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The inner workings of the document that I have not seen before I will not, I think, comment in detail, but I do see the list of garrisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a highly significant document, Mr. Liborius, as a military man, you would know that, wouldn't you?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The significance of the document you have produced, I don't think that I will, at this point in time, and on the screen, venture a comment with this very short time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Unable to comment on these documents then, as you are, or as you -- you say, would you agree that the conclusions drawn by you and the opinions mentioned by you in your statements to the Prosecution concerning the authority of General Cermak could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusions that are mentioned in my papers I stand by, as they are the result of my observations, my meetings in the field. You would suggest to play down the General Gotovina -- Cermak to merely a clerk. What I observed, and I described that in my conclusions, was another person. My question, in my own eyes now, is if you play him so much down, why on earth would he have meetings? With not only ECMM, UN teams as well. It wouldn't make any sense. But that was not what I observed in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Because, quite simply, as you said, he was a point of contact. Did you have any other generals' or commanders' phone numbers?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in my immediate possession.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you given any other generals' or commanders' phone numbers?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was given the phone numbers of some commanders, the Benkovac commander, but I was not given the phone numbers of other generals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Benkovac commander of what?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The meeting mentioned in one of the previous ECMM reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, may this document be made an exhibit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D772, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And may we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And it should -- I should admit it into evidence. That's what I'm doing now. D772 is admitted into evidence. The previous one as well, that misses on the transcript but I'm to be blamed for that myself by speaking too quickly. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. 65 ter 3460, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document dated the 23rd of August, 1995, from the Split Military District forward command post. And it's about the engagement of forces for the Knin 95 task. And it's an order to provide prompt and full security for the journey of the president of the Republic through the zone of responsibility of the Split Military District, and the visit of the president was something that you noted in your notes. This order, if we turn to page 2, concerns the various units and forces, to be used for the security of this matter in and around Knin. So a -- an operation on the ground, in Knin, requiring troops to perform a particular task and function of a non-operational character. Do you understand that? Go to page 3, 4, if we just flick through this document, it is all in those terms. And we get to the end of the document. And take it from me, the garrison command and General Cermak is nowhere to be seen in this document. All right? And this document goes to Operation Group North, South, and, on the last page, the 204th and the 113th. A non-operational matter like those other matters we have seen, Mr. Liborius, and nothing to do with General Cermak and the Knin garrison command to order those troops to undertake that task. Again, doesn't that indicate your conclusions as being erroneous and not based on fact?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: You highlight the tasks associated with this particular train ride. Where they'd say operational or non-operational, large undertaking, I will not comment. What I do note is that in my own assessment of General Gotovina and General Cermak, I did hold General Gotovina higher, so to speak, than General Gotovina -- General Cermak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That wasn't my question.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your -- your use of this particular document, I think, actually supports that, but I will, as I said before, refrain from speculating at this point in time over the whole corpus of the documents. I will reproduce, to the best of my knowledge, what I saw as the security structures, the law and order structures, and what I felt in field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We've heard your evidence and that is why I'm asking questions about it and challenging those points of views.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: May this document be made an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit number D773, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D773 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The last one and I have taken a selection here to inform you of this, Mr. Liborius, of different themes that have been brought in by you, and the next one I turn to is communications because that, you said, was significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So can we produce 2D01-0040.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is a document called the communications plan, Military District Split, forward command post Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It was the first page I wanted, which is just to show communications plan ZP Split-Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Doesn't matter. I can still deal with this, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This is the communications plan and perhaps the clerk of the court could just scroll through the pages that we have there, if this is the first page that has come up in the electronic system, and just scroll through them one by one. Ah, that's what I look for. Just to identify the document. That's my page 1. Maybe we can just turn to the next page to see the date, Knin, 13th of August, 1995. Yes. And it's the list of documents contained in the communications plan of the Split Military District. And we go to the next page. It gives the communications centres. Command communications. Nine of 18, it shows the code-names of the various Operational Groups of South. 11 of 18 shows identification codes for the ZP Military District Split offices. You probably know what I'm going to be saying, there is no mention here of the Knin garrison command, Knin ZM, General Cermak, anything at all. If we go to 15 of 18, work plan, various units we will have seen before. It's a lengthy document, but the point arising from your evidence is of significance. We have no need to go further through it. The Bench can look at in their own leisure. You mention communications as being a very important item to show command because when you were let you through a check-point, you thought that that gave an indication of how command and control, which could have led to General Cermak, proved your point. What do you say to the fact that the Knin ZM, Zborno Mjesto, General Cermak's garrison, isn't even in the communications plan for the Military District. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could come as no surprise to you -- it would come as no surprise to you that I would have the same position. What I asked myself when I have seen all the documents you have shown me is that General Gotovina, then, is frequently the signer of the documents. That would suggest that, then, he is the one having the command --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, Mr. Liborius. There's no need to dwell upon matters as if Mr. Cermak is not mentioned who else would -- that's not part of the question. And I ask you to refrain from further comments apart from answering the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer then. But in our meeting on the 27th of October, General Gotovina pointed to General Cermak to answer for the questions who were arrested. So there is this link between --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, the question is about communications and whether Mr. Cermak appears anywhere in the documents related to communications. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I take it that if Mr. Kay has perused the document and General Cermak is not in the document, I will rely on Mr. Kay's perusal of the document. We can walk around this for a long time. What I'm doing is that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, you're supposed to answer the questions and I see that you are taking great effort in doing that. Please proceed, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You see, the point is that you have presented a conclusion. I have put significant documents to you that have caused you to challenge in your own mind your conclusion about General Cermak. That's right, isn't it? That's what you want to admit?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't challenge my conclusions. What I do is that I produce, reproduce, each time General Cermak pops up in my monitoring activity, sometimes together with General Gotovina. When these two --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think you answered the last question of Mr. Kay --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and he will certainly put his next question to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May that be admitted as an exhibit, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit D774.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D774 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have access to any of the articles or interviews concerning General Cermak in the Croatian press at the time?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Press reviews were usually done by either the Croatian assistance team or -- located in ECMM headquarters in Zagreb or our local interpreters. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The question was did you --

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have access to any of the articles? I'm in the middle of answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Well, yes or no, did you read any -- any newspaper interviews concerning General Cermak's job as described by him at the time.

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Newspaper articles specifically on General Cermak, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For the Court's reference, it's D37 of significance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The topic I'm going to deal with you now which is his actual job, what he was actually doing, how he was spending his time and, again, I'm going to put a description to you and I'd like you to consider it and give answer to the Court. His job, put simply, was to restore normal life to Knin. To clear up the town, get the town working, and deal with problems that the UN faced in relation to their presence in Sector South. As simple as that. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did say that he should assist in restoring normal life. He did say that we could bring it to his attention if we saw problems in the field, security problems, looting and burning and that stuff, and General Gotovina said that security measures, who had been arrested and so on, we should turn to General Cermak. Restoring normal life is quite a wide word.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Should we look at what he was doing then, because that might indicate what his job was, don't you agree? For instance, if you're fixing the water, the electricity, cleaning the streets, it doesn't look as though your job is that of being a military commander, does it?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are handling issues of arrest and security guards then you are handling security. Doesn't it look like that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So your mind is this, that if one detail of security guards are sent to your office, that that is sufficient to demonstrate command and control over all the troops in the Sector South region? Is that honestly your judgement? Is that how you base your judgement?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I have given a host of examples of how security matters were brought to General Cermak. What we observed in the field was that he was designated as the person that you should meet, I think also human rights action teams and others, I believe. So if I understand your words right, that we should look at what he was doing, well, we were actually looking at what he was doing. We observed it. And he did attend, in many, many, meetings not only with ECMM but also with UN, to those questions. Whether he was attending to garbage cleaning, as you said, or cleaning the streets, electricity fixing, on top of that, well, I will not challenge that. I will not challenge -- I had not -- I will not challenge that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, for various purposes, I think we should stop a bit earlier than 6.00, if only for the traffic jams on the Dutch roads. Could you wrap up in a couple of minutes? Could you find a suitable moment to conclude for the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Next document I'll produce is 65 ter 236. And it's the report from this Major Jonjic, whom we have seen General Cermak needed some assistants to have working for him as a logistics officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: And this is Major Jonjic's report issued at some time, we don't have a date on it, but a description of his various tasks and what he was doing, revitalizing the age-old Croatian city. Seek out water, dealt with the hospital. Page 2 deals with the trains. Provides cars to the hospital. Page 3, dirt, epidemiological condition. Don't ask me to spell it. And arranging a welcome for the president, et cetera. So a survey there of his particular work and he was describing himself as the assistant to the garrison commander. So at that level. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Assistant to the garrison commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yeah. Dealing with cleaning the streets, getting the kindergarten going, the hospital, all these basic tasks. Were you aware that that was the backbone of the work of General Cermak in Knin?

utterances.speaker: SOREN LIBORIUS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, General Cermak himself said, I'm responsible for bringing back law and order to Knin. Order would perhaps also entail all these lists of tasks. I haven't seen the document here, before now, and as it will come as no surprise to you, I think I will, at this point in time, refrain from going into the details of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would that be a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That's a convenient moment, Your Honour. May that document be admitted, I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit number D775.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Liborius, out of an abundance of caution, we stop a bit earlier in order to make sure that you'll not miss your plane. Which, of course, brings us to the next issue; that is, we'd like to see you back because the -- your testimony has not yet been concluded. Now we asked Mr. Waespi earlier to discuss with you your presence on the 6th and the 7th of November this year, both dates high on your list of priorities. That would be Thursday 6th and Friday, 7th of November. Would you come to The Hague on those days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would prefer Friday, 7. As I indicated, bringing in two days of regular court sessions, I propose that we would instead take a day like this, combine two in one day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Liborius, how much time we would have in this Tribunal, in which, sometimes, where we have three courtrooms and sometimes six or seven cases at the same time, is still to be considered. Therefore, I do see your preference for the 7th. At the same time, if we would not finish in one day, and, again, I don't know whether we would have the whole of the day. We will certainly try to accommodate your concerns. Then it would bring us to the weekend and then, of course, we would have another problem; that is, whether or not you should stay over the weekend and whether -- so, therefore, the Chamber has a clear and explicit preference for the 6th. And of course, I can't hide from you that of course it is, to some extent, also in your own hands. I pointed a couple of times at -- at answers that certainly could have been shorter and I invited the parties also to put focussed questions to you. So, therefore, if we start on the 6th of November, whether we could perhaps with prolonged sessions, which still has to be seen whether that is possible, whether we could finish on that day is uncertain. But I would like you to keep yourself available the 6th and 7th of November.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will take it back and I will certainly do my utmost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Liborius, now just for your information, because this is not a clear, I'll make myself available these two days. If we could not finish the cross-examination, either it would urge us to ask you to come back again, which takes travelling, et cetera. It is expensive and takes additional time; or we might end up in a situation where the Chamber could not exclude that the Defence would argue that because you could not have been examined in full that therefore all of your evidence should be stricken from the record. I'm not saying that the Defence will do that but I already inform you that the Chamber cannot exclude that such an action, and whatever the outcome would be, would be taken. And I take it you, neither your government, would wish to us be in a situation where we would have to consider such a request. I said, I take it, if you say no, that's the situation I wish to come up, then of course I would like to hear from you. You see it is really important. You have given five statements, you have been examined quite lengthy for what we call a 92 ter witness, that is a witness who has given already evidence in statements that took quite sometime. We are slowly moving forward. Perhaps we could move forward a bit quicker. The Chamber would like you to be available on the 6th and the 7th. Is that clear to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You will be informed by the Victims and Witness Section when we will start on the 6th and we will try to accommodate you, to the extent possible, to see that it does not take more effort and more time and the Chamber appreciates the time you have spent until now on giving testimony in -- before this Tribunal. Then I again would like to instruct you, but now for a longer period of time, that you should not speak with anyone about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given on the 6th and perhaps on the 7th of November. You are excused. Yes, Mr. Liborius.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you for your consideration for the before 6.00. I just want to thank for you that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps Mr. Liborius could already be escorted out of the courtroom so that he can travel as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have some although, well, limited time left. We could perhaps deal with the exhibits that were tendered on the list by the Prosecution. Looking at this list, are there any objections against documents appearing on the list? Otherwise I will ask Mr. Registrar to read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I -- I have to look quickly. There was one exhibit that we objected to. I don't know if it is being tendered by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, and I withdraw our request to have it tendered and I believe this was 65 ter 5418.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that is withdrawn, from what I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you perhaps slowly read the -- first, the 65 ter numbers, then the provisionally assigned exhibit number. I don't know whether they changed due to the withdrawal of this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you have one second. Meanwhile, I inform the parties that for cross-examination, and I'm fully aware of the problems that we'll still have to find the schedules, but that the Chamber wants to conclude the cross-examination of Witness Liborius on not later than the 7th of November. Despite all the problems, we have to perhaps adapt to that to some extent. Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I have had a brief consultation with Mr. Cayley and my estimate will come down now in terms of my time. I obviously have to see where I have gone and what I need to challenge. I can think of one matter but I can deal with it perhaps in quite an easy way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I take it that Defence counsel together will compare how much time is still needed perhaps even briefly talk to Mr. Waespi what re-examination time would be needed. The Chamber, through the legal officers, might also give an input to reserve a certain amount of time so that we -- but, of course, that makes primarily sense once we know how much time there is available on the 6th and 7th of November. But even if it would just be two ordinary sessions, that is, two morning sessions or two afternoon sessions, that the testimony of this witness should conclude within these two days.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then I have a list in front of me -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Registry will file a list in which you'll find the 65 ter numbers. They are listed and they are not in sequential order, but the first one on the list is 5413. The last one on the list, the 26th, will be 4087. There are no objections against the documents under -- known under the 65 ter numbers on this list from the Defence. Therefore, the Chamber decides that these documents, all the documents on the list, 26 in number, will be admitted -- are admitted into evidence as Exhibits P831 up to and including P856. If there would be any problem with this at any later stage, the Chamber would like to hear, not later than by next Tuesday. Now, there is one matter and I have to check that carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. KUZMANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the videos are -- still need some attention. Mr. Waespi, are the full videos on the list or are they not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, they are. In fact, the previous Registrar has prepared a list as directed by you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then I have to -- as a matter of fact, I have to make a reservation because whether tendering the full videos is something the Chamber wishes -- whether they admit the full videos, more or less condemning the Chamber to spend their weekends behind the screen rather than to do anything else, we would still like to consider that. Therefore, the full videos are provisionally -- no, let me just see. Yes, they are preceding this list and now I'm really confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I believe --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because we had a list of videos which run from P821 up to and including P833.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the Chamber has no problem in admitting into evidence the video-clips we have seen; there are nine of them. But the Chamber wants to consider whether we will admit into evidence the full videos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MISETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am advised by my case manager that the numbers there are wrong and that these numbers have already been now reassigned to other exhibits and we need to -- on this list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just see. I see that -- yes, I see, as a matter of fact, that the full videos are on the new list. The first one being 3763, P846, if -- the second one -- can't find them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the video-clips are included. It becomes a bit chaotic now. Mr. Registrar will file the list. We'll then see whether the decision yet taken needs reconsideration and the Chamber expresses already on the record that it reserves its decision on the full video going beyond the clips that were shown in court. Let not try to further work this out because it might even lead to more chaos. If there are any practical problems in relation to the list, could you please first address Mr. Monkhouse so that he can prepare whatever the Chamber would have to consider before we continue. Then are there any other procedural matters at this moment? If not, then we adjourn, and we will resume on Monday, the 15th of September, 9.00 in the morning, Courtroom I.
